clue.text: Bird we might see in Walton ?

definitions.text: Bird we might see in Walton ?

parts.words: Bird we might see in Walton ?
parts.note: Izaak Walton wrote The Compleat Angler, so he was a champion of anglers: a monarch among fishermen, which also names a bird

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher wonders what species turns up in the town of Walton.
explanation.walkthrough: Walton is Izaak Walton, the seventeenth-century author of The Compleat Angler; as the greatest of anglers he is the 'king fisher', and the bird of that name dives for fish too.
explanation.definitionFit: The kingfisher is a small bright-blue bird that dives into rivers to catch fish.

clue.text: A: punt? What a thrill!

explanation.surface: An exclamation of delight about a boat outing on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: A punt looks like the flat river boat, but here it is a kick of the ball dropped from the hands, as in rugby; 'What a kick!' is said of a thrill.
explanation.definitionFit: A punt is one sort of kick in football, and a kick is also a buzz of excitement.

clue.text: Book featuring local anaesthetics?

explanation.surface: A volume that includes drugs for deadening pain.
explanation.walkthrough: Things that numb could be called 'numb-ers'; the same letters name the fourth book of the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: Numbers is a book of the Bible, and local anaesthetics deaden feeling, so they make you numb.

clue.text: Novel by outspoken Essex opener on tennis reform

parts.note: someone outspoken is frank

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter, here of Essex
reform means form again in a new shape, so the letters of tennis are rearranged

explanation.surface: A book written by a forthright Essex opening batsman about changing the rules of tennis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essex opener' looks like a cricketer from the English county of Essex, but it is just the letter E; 'reform' rearranges TENNIS into NSTEIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Shelley's 1818 Gothic novel tells of a scientist who builds a creature from corpses.

clue.text: Bears us up as it changes directions

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word us is read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: changes tells us the letters of as and it alter their order

parts.note: N and S are the compass directions north and south

explanation.surface: Something supports us as its course keeps shifting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns US into SU; 'changes' rearranges AS IT into STAI; then come N and S.
explanation.definitionFit: To sustain a load is to carry or support it, as a beam bears weight.

clue.text: The Spanish-French river girl

parts.note: el is the Spanish for the
the Oise is a river in northern France, a tributary of the Seine

explanation.surface: A girl from a river on the Spanish-French border.
explanation.definitionFit: A female first name, as in the medieval lover of Abelard.

clue.text: Pass for workman

explanation.surface: Something hands a pass to a labourer, or a pass masquerades as a workman.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass something is to hand it over; a hand is also a manual labourer, as in farmhand or deckhand.

clue.text: Returning about one to rent a studio

indicators.note: returning means the whole string of pieces is read backwards, coming back up the column

parts.note: re means about, concerning
the Roman numeral for one is I
to let a property is to rent it out

explanation.surface: Someone coming back to take a lease on an artist's studio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning' acts on all four pieces at once, so the whole string is read from the bottom of the column up.
explanation.definitionFit: An atelier is an artist's or designer's workshop.

clue.text: Named the flier in poor Eddie's case

indicators.note: in tells us the insect goes inside the rearranged letters
poor signals that the letters of Eddie's are to be rearranged

parts.note: a gnat is a small flying insect

explanation.surface: An aviator is identified in the lawsuit brought by unfortunate Eddie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' signals the anagram of the name with its S, and 'in' puts the insect inside; 'case' only completes the picture of a container.
explanation.definitionFit: To designate is to name or appoint someone officially.

clue.text: Ship's guide meets no one coming back-pity

parts.note: a ship is steered by its compass

indicators.note: coming back tells us to read the two little words no and one in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: A navigator's instrument meets nobody returning, which is a sad thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming back' applies only to 'no one', which is split into its two words before being turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Compassion is sympathy and sorrow for another's suffering, much the same feeling as pity.

clue.text: Notes performers of opening turns

explanation.surface: A memo about the people who do the first acts in a variety show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening turns' looks like the first acts at a music hall, but it is the turning a key does in a lock to open it.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical key is a set of related notes, and a key turned in a lock opens a door.

clue.text: The order all barons, counts, dukes, etc, exemplify

definitions.text: The order all barons, counts, dukes, etc, exemplify

parts.words: The order all barons, counts, dukes, etc, exemplify
parts.note: looks like an order of nobility, but the words all, barons, counts, dukes, etc begin with a, b, c, d, e in sequence

explanation.surface: A question about the order of precedence among the ranks of the nobility.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a ranking of the peerage, yet the five words simply start with the first five letters in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Listed like the letters A to E, in dictionary sequence.

clue.text: Feeble for a time, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the word for the time is to be taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: a week is a span of time, seven days

explanation.surface: Someone has been feeble for a while, or so the rumour goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Weak and feeble both describe something lacking strength.

clue.text: Pardoning Jack taking your job on ?

parts.note: a jack is a sailor, and AB (able-bodied seaman) is the usual crossword abbreviation for a sailor
your job on this puzzle is the work of working out its clues

explanation.surface: A forgiving man named Jack takes over your work while you are away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'your job on ?' means your job on this crossword, which is cracking it.
explanation.definitionFit: To absolve someone is to forgive them formally, so absolving is granting a pardon.

clue.text: Trespass on the ground of an ill-natured person ?

definitions.text: Trespass on the ground of an ill-natured person ?

parts.words: Trespass on the ground of an ill-natured person ?
parts.note: to trespass is to go across someone's plot of land, so to cross a patch

explanation.surface: Someone intrudes on the land of a grumpy neighbour.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as CROSS PATCH: crossing a patch of ground is trespassing; the whole word is an old name for a bad-tempered person.
explanation.definitionFit: A crosspatch is a grumpy, irritable person.

clue.text: Ringing about drunkard embracing poor Ann

parts.note: re means about, concerning

indicators.note: embracing means the word for the drunkard wraps round the other piece

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunk

indicators.note: poor signals that the letters of Ann are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is phoning about a drunk who is hugging unfortunate Ann.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' rearranges the name, and 'embracing' has the drunkard wrap round it; 'Ringing' looks like a phone call but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something resonant echoes and reverberates, as a ringing bell does.

clue.text: A Tibetan phrase, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals a possible rearrangement of the letters of the word beside it

explanation.surface: Someone offers what might be a saying from Tibet.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherpas are a mountain people of Tibetan descent living in the Himalayas of Nepal.

clue.text: Perhaps cigar men of a continental country

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of cigar men are one possible arrangement of other letters

explanation.surface: Perhaps the men smoking cigars come from somewhere in Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Germanic means relating to Germany, a country on the European continent.

clue.text: Hardy character's birthplace?

parts.note: reads as the hometown of someone in a Thomas Hardy novel, but a hardy character is a tough, austere person, a word that comes from an ancient Greek city-state

explanation.surface: A literary question about where one of Thomas Hardy's figures was born.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital H makes us think of Thomas Hardy, but it is only the first word. A tough, frugal person is called Spartan, after the citizens of this city.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek city-state was famous for raising tough, frugal warriors, giving us the adjective for an austere person.

clue.text: Girl of foreign type gets in a row

indicators.note: gets in says the foreign word slips inside the other pieces

parts.note: a line is a row
de is French and Spanish for of, so the foreign version of the word of

explanation.surface: A girl from abroad joins a queue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of foreign type' asks for the word 'of' in a foreign language, here French or Spanish; 'gets in' slips it between the article and the row.
explanation.definitionFit: A female first name, familiar from the old song Sweet Adeline.

clue.text: Going over the main repair base, Nore settlement

indicators.note: repair suggests mending by putting the parts back together differently, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A naval ship crosses the sea to a repair base at the Nore anchorage.
explanation.walkthrough: The Nore is a sandbank and anchorage in the Thames estuary that was once a Royal Navy station; 'repair' rearranges BASE and NORE.
explanation.definitionFit: The main is the open sea, so something carried across it is ocean-borne, travelling by ship.

clue.text: Eastern port a centre for navy? Get away!

indicators.note: centre for says the little word a becomes the middle of the navy's abbreviation

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy
go on! and get away! are both cries of disbelief

explanation.surface: A naval hub in the east, greeted with disbelief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get away!' is the exclamation of disbelief, the same as 'Go on!'
explanation.definitionFit: Rangoon, now Yangon, is the chief port of Myanmar, formerly Burma, in Asia.

clue.text: Rae gets nothing back for this accelerator

indicators.note: back says the name Rae and the word for nothing together are read backwards, up the column

parts.note: nil means nothing, zero

explanation.surface: Rae gets nothing in return for a particle accelerator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the name and the word for nothing round together; the definition is the kind of particle accelerator the answer describes.
explanation.definitionFit: A linear accelerator speeds particles along a straight path, as opposed to a circular one.

clue.text: Red-heads in committee?

parts.note: looks like ginger-haired people meeting, but reds are communists and their heads would be the Soviet leadership body

explanation.surface: A meeting of people with ginger hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red' means communist, and the heads of Soviet government sat on a standing executive body of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Soviet Union a standing executive council acted for the legislature between its sessions.

clue.text: " A ship, an ——, a sickle moon " (Flecker)

definitions.text: " A ship, an ——, a sickle moon " (Flecker)

parts.words: " A ship, an ——, a sickle moon " (Flecker)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: the missing word in the line from James Elroy Flecker's poem

explanation.surface: A line of poetry by James Elroy Flecker with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line opens Flecker's poem A Ship, an Isle, a Sickle Moon; fill the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem pictures a vessel, a small island and a crescent moon.

clue.text: Come down by excursion ?

explanation.surface: Someone descends on an outing.
explanation.walkthrough: To trip is to stumble and fall, and a trip is also a short outing; 'by' only joins the two.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripping makes you fall to the ground, and a trip is a jaunt or outing.

clue.text: Prince indisposed to meet debts-fatal

indicators.note: indisposed means unwell, out of sorts, so the letters of Prince are put out of order

parts.note: IOUs are written promises to repay, so debts

explanation.surface: An ailing royal has to settle what he owes, with deadly consequences.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pernicious is deadly or gravely harmful.

clue.text: Careful attention on the editor's part

indicators.note: part says the answer is only a portion of the letters running through the editor's words

explanation.surface: The editor is expected to be meticulous.
explanation.definitionFit: To pay heed is to give close notice or regard to something.

clue.text: Possibly uncle breaks temporary peace through aggressiveness

indicators.note: breaks says the rearranged letters break into the word for a short peace

parts.note: a truce is a temporary cessation of fighting

indicators.note: possibly signals that uncle is a possible version of other letters, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An uncle ends a ceasefire by being belligerent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges the relative, and 'breaks' sends those letters into the ceasefire word just before its final letter; 'through' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Truculence is a fierce, defiant readiness to fight or argue.
